question: Has road safety for pedestrians in Brooklyn gotten better since 2013? Make a chart suitable for a local news story and summarize the findings.

options.metric: Annual number of pedestrians injured in police-reported Brooklyn crashes
options.reason: Injury counts directly measure the reported nonfatal pedestrian harm and provide a clear year-by-year trend.
options.answer: Reported Brooklyn pedestrian injuries declined from 3,641 in 2013 to 2,835 in 2025 (22.1% lower), though they rose from a low of 1,781 in 2020.
options.interpretation: This framing answers whether annual reported nonfatal pedestrian injuries improved: counts declined from 3,641 in 2013 to 1,781 in 2020, then rose to 2,835 in 2025. Injury counts directly measure reported harm but not risk per walking trip. It leaves deaths, pedestrian exposure, and the reasons for the trend unanswered. Rows with NULL borough were omitted (share of all rows by plotted year, 2013–2025: 2013: 23.4%, 2014: 24.1%, 2015: 24.9%, 2016: 33.3%, 2017: 38.1%, 2018: 35.6%, 2019: 35.2%, 2020: 34.7%, 2021: 34.7%, 2022: 33.8%, 2023: 32.0%, 2024: 28.6%, 2025: 19.9%); no Brooklyn rows have NULL pedestrian injury or death counts, and the partial 2012 (July–December) and 2026 (January 1–June 11) years were excluded.

options.metric: Annual number of pedestrians killed in police-reported Brooklyn crashes
options.reason: Fatalities are the most severe outcome and can move differently from nonfatal injuries.
options.answer: Reported Brooklyn pedestrian deaths rose from 30 in 2013 to 39 in 2025 (30.0% higher), with sizable year-to-year fluctuations.
options.interpretation: This framing answers whether the most severe reported pedestrian outcome improved: annual death counts fluctuated and were higher in 2025 (39) than in 2013 (30). Fatality counts capture severity that injury counts cannot. It leaves nonfatal injury burden, risk per walking trip, and the reasons for changes unanswered. Rows with NULL borough were omitted (share of all rows by plotted year, 2013–2025: 2013: 23.4%, 2014: 24.1%, 2015: 24.9%, 2016: 33.3%, 2017: 38.1%, 2018: 35.6%, 2019: 35.2%, 2020: 34.7%, 2021: 34.7%, 2022: 33.8%, 2023: 32.0%, 2024: 28.6%, 2025: 19.9%); no Brooklyn rows have NULL pedestrian injury or death counts, and the partial 2012 (July–December) and 2026 (January 1–June 11) years were excluded.

options.metric: Brooklyn crash rows with at least one pedestrian injured or killed per 1,000 Brooklyn crash rows
options.denominator: All Brooklyn police-reported crash rows in the same year
options.reason: The per-crash share accounts for changes in the volume of Brooklyn crash reports while measuring how often reported crashes involve pedestrian harm.
options.answer: Pedestrian-harm crashes increased from 74.4 per 1,000 Brooklyn crash rows in 2013 to 113.8 in 2025 (53.0% higher), despite fewer total Brooklyn crash rows.
options.interpretation: This framing answers how often reported Brooklyn crashes involved pedestrian injury or death: the rate fell from 74.4 per 1,000 in 2013 to 56.8 in 2017, then rose to 113.8 in 2025. Using all Brooklyn crash rows as the denominator adjusts for changes in reported crash volume. It leaves risk per walking trip and changes in exposure or reporting completeness unanswered. Rows with NULL borough were omitted (share of all rows by plotted year, 2013–2025: 2013: 23.4%, 2014: 24.1%, 2015: 24.9%, 2016: 33.3%, 2017: 38.1%, 2018: 35.6%, 2019: 35.2%, 2020: 34.7%, 2021: 34.7%, 2022: 33.8%, 2023: 32.0%, 2024: 28.6%, 2025: 19.9%); no Brooklyn rows have NULL pedestrian injury or death counts, and the partial 2012 (July–December) and 2026 (January 1–June 11) years were excluded.

answer:
Reported Brooklyn pedestrian injuries fell 22.1%, from 3,641 in 2013 to 2,835 in 2025, but rose from a low of 1,781 in 2020 (chart: `out/option_1.png`).
Reported pedestrian deaths rose 30%, from 30 in 2013 to 39 in 2025, with substantial year-to-year fluctuations (chart: `out/option_2.png`).
Crashes involving pedestrian injury or death increased from 74.4 to 113.8 per 1,000 Brooklyn crash rows between 2013 and 2025, but this is not a risk-per-walking-trip measure (chart: `out/option_3.png`).
